speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yesterday, when the hon. member for Fundy-Royal proposed to move this motion, the Chair drew the attention of hon. members to a difficulty in relation to the form of the third report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments.
I think I should insist on the fact that it is not the substance of the report which concerns the Chair, but rather its form. As I stated yesterday, there is a procedure established by the House of Commons Act and the supply legislation for the employment of committee staff. The method suggested in this case appears to the Chair to be inconsistent with that observed in the past. I am aware, however, that arrangements have been made in the other place to overcome the difficulty, and I would think that in the circumstances it would be in order to put the motion.
I might also add that, as the hon. member for Fundy-Royal pointed out yesterday, there have been consultations of which I was not aware, which puts a different complexion on the situation. I have to assume that this motion is being put by consent, so it will not necessarily constitute a precedent. This having been said, I am sure hon. members will expect the Chair to put the motion.

subsubtopic: INTENTION OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF CONTINGENCY PLAN TO DEAL WITH INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has said that Bill C-29, the so-called anti-profiteering bill, is not an anti-inflation bill and is not a price control measure. On the other hand, the Minister of Finance has told the House that it is not part of the government's contingency plan. I ask the Prime Minister whether it is still the government's intention to institute its contingency plan dealing with inflation rather than limiting itself to a bill such as Bill C-29 which has found so little favour in the House?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INTENTION OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF CONTINGENCY PLAN TO DEAL WITH INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the logic of the question escapes me because it assumes that price and wage control, which is the contingency plan, would find the favour of the House and I am doubtful also that that would happen. Perhaps the Tories will have a chance to speak about it on the hustings. I am quite certain it is not the right approach to inflation and, more importantly, it is not the best approach to profiteering.

May 3, 1974

As the hon. member knows, the bill is attacking special cases of gouging or profiteering, whereas the approach to which he alludes, that of the contingency plan, is an over-all freeze. As the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion indicated yesterday, it is not an approach that we favour. We do not want to put a freeze on the wages of the small earners.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I take it the minister is suggesting common procedure. speechtext:
Order. Before proceeding to the consideration of the four motions to amend Bill C-19, the Chair would like to express some concern as to the regularity of motion No. 2 in the name of the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher). As the hon. member knows, a similar motion was submitted on October 24, 1973, and was ruled to be irregular. I thought I should mention this immediately so that the hon. member, whenever we reach motion No.

2, might be prepared, if he so wishes, to attempt to convince the Chair that on this occasion it should be accepted.
There may be some reservations on the part of the Chair in relation to motions three and four-I do not think they are so serious that we ought to embark on a procedural argument at this point; in due course they might be put, unless objection is taken to doing so. For the moment, the Chair will put motion No. 1.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIONS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Motion No 1.
That Bill C-19 be amended by deleting clause seven and renumbering the subsequent clauses accordingly.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising once again to debate this subject, which, as you know, was raised back in October of last year, let me begin by saying this: it is my view that any time a piece of legislation fails to pass in a given session, then no matter what its political complexion might be, the government should at least consider seriously the criticisms which have been directed toward that legislation, and some attempt should be made to reach a compromise.
Needless to say, I am very disappointed that no effort has been made to reach a compromise in this situation, though I believe one could have been achieved. Someone once said that politics was the art of compromise. This may or may not be true, but if legislation is to get through in a minority House a certain amount of compromise is sometimes necessary. No effort whatsoever has been made in connection with the subject before us.
I was unable to attend the proceedings during committee stage because that committee sat at the same time as the transportation committee of which I am the chairman. But I did read the committee reports dealing with clause 7, the subject of the motion now before the House. Here again I was utterly amazed to find there were no questions asked. No member from either side of the House attempted to make a compromise with the opposition on this particular clause of the bill. Clauses 8 to 12 were passed with the chairman of the committee asking "Shall sections 8 to 12 pass?" As I say, those clauses were passed with not a question asked.
I came to parliament some 16 years ago as a naive westerner, a country boy or whatever other term might be applied. But I came here with a deep trust and belief in democracy.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIONS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: You are just like every other country boy, Jack.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIONS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I believed that if a person had a point of view, in a democracy that point of view should be heard. If there is a point of view across the country, then in a democracy that point of view should be heard. Needless to say, I was deeply disappointed with the members of the Conservative party who were in the committee and who failed to mention clauses 8 to 12 when they knew in their hearts they had made no effort to compromise on this particular part of the legislation.

They knew of their failing at the first attempt to pass this bill. On that occasion I said that the two religious sects to which clause 7 gives exemption from the Canada Pension Plan should appear before the committee and state why they felt they should get out. On the first hearing of this bill in the last session, the committee thought they were very clever. I left the committee on the wishes of the Conservative party whip to come to this House to make a speech on the CNR financing bill, and as soon as I left the committee said no, they did not want the Hutterian sect from Alberta to appear before the committee, that they would pass the bill. They did not say that verbally but that was the upshot of it. They said "That maverick Horner from Crowfoot," as the press calls me, "has gone, so we can now pass the bill".
On second reading of the bill in this House I said that I would attempt to block the bill again. I had nothing below the table. I had hoped at that time that the leaders of the Conservative party, the House leader, or somebody, would attempt to reach a compromise. I had hoped that the member in charge of health and welfare in the shadow cabinet would attempt to reach a compromise. I also said at that time that I hoped they would not make the mistake that they made in the last session and would have these two religious groups appear before the committee to state why they wanted out of the plan. As I said earlier, I did not have the chance to attend the committee because I had certain obligations as chairman of the transport committee.
I must say I am sorely disappointed in the so-called art of politics, the art of compromise, that exists among the parties on this particular measure. I have no hesitation in saying that, having read the press clippings of the debate in the last session when I spoke on this issue. I have before me a press clipping from the Globe and Mail for September 15, 1973 which states this:
Hutterites are the "very finest of Canadians," Heath Macquarrie (PC, Hillsborough) said yesterday in a Commons speech apparently intended as a rebuff for fellow Conservative Jack Horner (Crowfoot)-
-the Hutterite tradition of providing for their older members is a practice that has disappeared throughout society in general.
I thought that an interesting remark for the hon. member to make. The hon. member spoke in the House on the guaranteed annual income measure. Few of us today, outside of the Hutterian sect, care for our elderly citizens and leave that for the government. It is not the fault of the people that some of them have failed to take care of their elderly; it is the fault of the politicians who say: "We can do better, leave it to us. We can tax you and make certain your elderly will be taken care of". That is really what the Canada Pension Plan is saying. It is not saying: "You have a choice to be taxed or not to be taxed". It is saying: "You will be taxed". It is saying: "We the government, we the politicians, know you will not look after your elderly; we are going to make certain that they are looked after because we will tax you as you go along through this life of ours". The government has made that choice.
The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) might like to come out to southern Alberta if he thinks it is only the maverick member for Crowfoot who is speaking this afternoon. If he thinks that I am not representing the voice of a group of concerned people across the prai-
Canada Pension Plan
ries, then I welcome him to come out to Crowfoot if an election is called next week. I will not sit on the same platform with him, but I welcome him to come to Crowfoot and to speak out for the Hutterites. I would even rent the hall for him. I will not heckle him but I will be there as an interested representative of the people so I can see their reaction to his remarks. So I issue that invitation to him. I know he is in the shadow cabinet of the great Conservative party and that the party will pay his expenses, so no expense will be incurred by him.
What are these people, Mr. Speaker, who are they, and how large a group are they? The government by this bill has declared their religion to be better than all others. First of all, who and what are they? I am dealing explicitly with the Hutterian group, because the Amish are a completely different group. While both might have come from the early Mennonite religion, the Amish are completely different because they ask nothing from our society. They take no advantages from our society. The Hutterites take every advantage that is available in our modern, technological age. If an acreage payment is due from the government, if there is a guaranteed wheat payment due from the minister representing the Canadian Wheat Board in this House, then they accept it. If there is a subsidy paid on butter, cream or something else by the government, then they accept it.
They are a religious order; there is no question of that. I have studied their religion and I find it quite interesting. They carry on a heavy farming industry. I just want to quote from the judgment of the Federal Court in which their case is presented. I am quoting from the Hutterians, own presentation to the court:
The Hutterites are organized in colonies of approximately 100 persons each. When the members of a colony decide that it has become too large for effective operation a small number of them will break off from the "mother" colony and with the financial and other material assistance thereof form a "daughter" colony. In the various documents which were tendered in evidence on the trial of the actions the colonies are described as congregations or communities and these congregations or communities are associated in groups known respectively as Darius-Leut, Lehrer-Leut and Schmeid-Leut. Generally speaking, residents in the colony are members of the Hutterian Brethren Church which was incorporated in Canada-
The judgment then goes on:
The objects of the Corporation shall be to engage in and carry on the Christian religion, Christian worship and religious education and teaching and to worship God according to the religious belief of the members of the Corporation ...
Each congregation or community of the Church is empowered, inter alia, as follows:
To engage in, and carry on farming, stock raising, milling, and all branches of these industries; and to manufacture and deal with the products and by-products of these industries;
To carry on any other business (whether manufacturing or otherwise) which may seem to said congregation or community of the said Church capable of being conveniently carried on in connection with its business or calculated directly or indirectly to enhance the property or rights of the congregation or community;
That makes it pretty clear. They, themselves, admit they are prepared to carry on the business of farming, of stock raising and manufacturing. We recognize that many other people in our society are prepared to carry on the business of stock raising, farming and manufacturing, in many

May 3, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
cases in opposition or in competition with them. I have maintained right along that Canada Pension Plan contributions are a form of tax placed upon all those doing business. During the last speech I made on this subject matter in this House I quoted from two dictionaries as to what the word "tax" meant, and I think I substantiated my case. Let me go a little further in my explanation of what I believe a tax is.
I believe that in essence this is a tax, and that a tax is something levied against people whether or not they themselves make a contribution. If I were an employer and hired men to work on my farm or in my manufacturing plant, I must make a deduction from the wages or salaries of those people for the Canada Pension Plan. I must do that whether I want to or not. The government of Canada has said I must make that deduction from those people I have working for me on my farm ranch. I must tax them under the Canada Pension Plan and send that to the government. Because I have them working for me I must take 1.8 per cent out of their salaries or wages and send that in, and another 1.8 per cent out of my profits and send that also to the government because this government believes it is its duty to take care of these people when they get old. To my way of thinking that is a tax. They are asking everyone to take a portion of their salaries or wages, and that is a tax. The Hutterians do not disagree about this question of paying taxes. The reason they want to get out of the Canada Pension Plan is based on something else, and I will get to that a little bit later.
In my last speech I quoted from a well-known author of Hutterian teachings and religious beliefs. He stated that they do not in any way disagree with having to pay taxes the governments levy upon them. This former writer of Hutterian teachings, Mr. Rideman, stated that quite clearly. He said this:
Since governmental authority is ordained by God and hath its office from Him, the payment of taxes for this purpose is likewise ordained and commanded, as Paul saith, "Thus ye must also pay tribute." For this reason we, likewise, willingly pay taxes, tribute or whatever men may term it, and in no way oppose it, for we have learned this from our Master, Christ, who not only paid it Himself, but also commanded others to do so, saying, "Render unto Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's."
One could go on reading from their teachings, but I want to make it abundantly clear that they, themselves, do not take any objection to the paying of taxes. They want out of the Canada Pension Plan for another reason, and not necessarily because of their own religious desires. They want out because under the Canada Pension Plan everyone must have a social security number so that contributions under the Canada Pension Plan can be properly recorded under that number. The Hutterian people do not want social security numbers.
How many thousands of other Canadians across Canada do not want a social security number? I would suggest there are thousands and thousands of Canadians across Canada who were repelled, and to this day do not like the idea of carrying around with them a number which is recorded in the computers of this and other governments. Many Canadians outside of the Hutterian religion have as yet not taken out a social security number. The government knows this. It writes them threatening letters telling them to take out social security numbers or action will be

taken against them. Such a letter has been written to my sister because she never took out a social security number. She never bowed to the big hand of the government, and to this day I do not think she has a social security number. She still makes contributions to the Canada Pension Plan as she has an income and she must under this law, but what happens to that money? I suggest it goes into the coffers of the government, into the Canada Pension Plan fund, but it will never be paid back to her and she knows that just as thousands of Canadians who have not taken out social security numbers know they will never receive benefits under this plan. Lots of lawyers across Canada have not got social security numbers and they know they will not receive the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan. These people feel this is their prerogative, that they have freedom of choice and they are prepared to pay something for that freedom. However, they are still being taxed.
The minister says that this involves only two small groups, so let us give them this privilege as it really will not matter very much. I do not intend to deal with how large the Amish group is but, as I have said before, they are quite different. They make no demands on our society. They do not make any contribution toward the development of new technology, but they do not take advantage of it either. The Hutterian people are completely different. They take advantage of every modern convenience available.
Let us consider how large a group this is. Let me start with Manitoba. There are approximately 5,000 Hutterian people in that province. They own or lease 178,000 acres, or did in 1972, and perhaps the figure is greater now. They practically own 170,000 acres and lease an additional 8,000 acres. They have 48 colonies in the province of Manitoba, or did in 1972, and that works out to an average of 3700 acres per colony. I would like to set my family up on 3700 acres of that rich heavily productive land in Manitoba. I would like to use the facilities of the hospitals and roads in Manitoba without having to pay taxes toward this Canada Pension Plan as do all the people in every province of Canada, except the province of Quebec which has a different system. The province of Quebec uses this pension fund very wisely and receives a 10 per cent return. I do not know whether that is an excess profit, but I will leave that to the government to determine.
In any case if my conscience would allow me I would like to farm on 3700 acres of that rich land in Manitoba. I could then provide well for my children, and I am sure they would provide for me when I get older, particularly if I did not have to pay taxes and could use the roads, the hospitals and other facilities provided by the Manitoba government. My conscience would not let me do that. My religious beliefs may not be as good as those of many other people in this House, or any better than those of the Hutterian people, but my conscience would not allow me to do that.
In the province of Saskatchewan there are 30 colonies, or were in 1972, with a total population of 2,500 people. They have 294,500 acres which works out to an average of 10,000 acres per colony, or just a shade under that. That is a very good sized operation, and what I said about the Hutterian situation in Manitoba applies equally in Saskatchewan. These people, too, use the hospitals and the

roads that the province of Saskatchewan builds from moneys borrowed from the federal government.
They fought to avoid paying income tax until last year when the income tax department ruled against them. They are ordained by this government as having some religion that is superior to that of anybody else. It may well be that it is superior to mine, but my conscience would not permit me to ask what they are requesting and what the government would give them under this piece of legislation. The government is capitulating in respect of their wishes. It may be that many people think their religion is better than mine, but as I have said my conscience would not permit to do what they are doing.
Let us look at the situation in the province of Alberta. One might study the history in respect of these people in the province of Alberta going back to 1923, 51 years ago. Anybody who has studied the history of the province of Alberta knows that this question has been a political thorn for every political party that has tried to function in that province. This government, which probably has studied this question a little, should have known about that history. It should have known this when it attempted to pass this bill the first time and failed. It should have known that it would have some difficulty if it attempted to do so a second time. There has been a failure even to attempt to reach a compromise on this situation. That has destroyed a little of my faith in the principles of democracy because certainly politics, as often has been said, in essence is the art of compromise.
In the province of Alberta, there were 82 colonies with a population of a little over 7,000 people in 1972. These figures may not be considered to be large in a province the size of Alberta. However, they control and own practically one million acres of land in that province. This is not a million acres of bushland or rock land. It is probably the best land available. It is the irrigated land in the south and the heavily productive land in the parkland regions of Alberta. This history of these people has not been one of pioneering the bushland or of going into the Peace River country. Because of the limitations in respect of land, over the years they have been forced to push their way into the Peace River country, but that has not been their custom. The Hutterite people know I speak the truth in this regard. The average colony occupies an area of approximately 20,000 acres or better. That is a nice size.
I might refer to the Alberta study in respect of the Community Properties Act of 1972. There is no suggestion that this is an anti-Hutterite report. Many people in Alberta might say it is the opposite. That report states quite clearly that the Hutterite population doubles every 17 years. We have heard much about a corporate rip-off and many people will wonder if the member for Crowfoot is trying to build a mountain out of a molehill or might suggest there are not that many of these people and, therefore, they do not effect society very much. This report states that the total produce sold by the Hutterite colonies in the province of Alberta in 1972 amounted in value to $23 million. The report also indicates that the total expenses of the Hutterite colonies in the province of Alberta were $17 million.
Canada Pension Plan
I know there was once a great politician, and in the eyes of many people perhaps a great Canadian, who stated, "What is a million". Well, here we are talking about a concern in one province, not in the three provinces I have mentioned, which sold produce with a value of $23 million. The report came out in 1972, but I think the figures cited are 1971 figures. I do not have to explain to anyone the comparison between the value of a dollar today and the value of a dollar in 1971. If they sold $23 million worth of produce in 1971 I do not think I would be out of the ball park if I said in terms of today's values that thev sold about $35 million worth of produce. It might also be considered that their expenses have risen as sharply or more sharply, but I point out these figures so that the House may be fully aware of what we are talking about. There is no question in my mind that we are dealing with a large enterprise. I dealt with the subject matter of whether it is a tax that is involved. I also dealt with the question of whether or not these people are willing to pay a tax. Then, I dealt with the amount of money and land involved.
Now I should like to refer again to the 1972 report. The $23 million worth of produce to which I referred in the year 1971 was equal to 3 per cent of the agricultural products produced and sold in that year in the whole province of Alberta. Well, we all know what 3 per cent is. If you take three times 30 the figure is close to 100 per cent. In the agricultural area of Alberta 7,000 people produce 3 per cent of the total agricultural produce sold in that province. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that I as a man who has throughout all his life been deeply interested in the agriculture industry should not be worried about competition in respect of agriculture? I am not afraid of competition, but I think it is the duty of the government to lay down rules so that competition is fair. If this is a tax upon me and my operation, then it should be a tax upon their operation. I do not deny these people the right of freedom of religion. The judge who presided over the court proceedings in September last year ruled that in no way would the income tax interfere with their right to carry on their religion.
If a judge of a federal court can decide in this regard that this does not in any way effect their freedom of religion, then that division has been made. One may ask why we should be concerned about this small amount of tax in respect of the Canada Pension Plan. It may be said that surely in a free enterprise society we can give our competitors a little bit of a leg-up and still survive. Undoubtedly all that is true.
However, it is the government's duty to lay down the law fairly. Many of my socialist friends in the House have suggested that we should all be given everything equally. I know we are not all born equal but in my opinion we should all be treated equally before the law in a democracy. The exemption granted to these people demonstrates clearly that we are not all treated equally before the law. In my opinion this is a mistake in a democracy. People should be treated equally no matter what their religion may be. The government is well aware of this. They took the Hutterites to court on a matter of income tax and the judge ruled in the government's favour.

May 3, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
I know that there is difficulty in taxing the Hutterites both under the Income Tax Act and the pension plan, because they do not allow their people to have any income. I do not deny that there is such a difficulty and, as I said in my earlier speeches on the subject, that is why the minister does not know how to go about taxing them. Well, it is pretty clear that the Department of National Revenue has not had that difficulty. At page 10 of the decision of the Federal Court of Canada of September, 1973 we find the following statement:
The Hutterites carry on efficient and successful farm operations. Financial statements filed, assuming they are typical of all or most of the colonies' operations, indicate that they have substantial net profits each year the taxability of which has led to these proceedings.
Apparently until 1960 the colony paid no income tax of any kind. I might point out that the Hutterites lost the case, and they will now be subject to income tax going as far back as 1961. I am thankful that the government proceeded on an issue which I started in the House in 1961. I saw the culmination of it 14 years later when the agricultural industry started being treated with greater fairness. The judgment goes on to read:
However, some time after 1960 assessments were levied at least against the corporate entities from which appeals were taken. Ultimately an agreement of understanding was entered into in 1968 between the Minister of National Revenue and certain of the appellants for and on behalf of the Hutterian Brethren colonies in Canada.
If this session lasts longer than we expect, I will put a question on the order paper requesting a copy of that agreement. I might find it interesting reading and I might find that they are all treated fairly. But to give you an idea of the size of their profits, in this particular case the judge stated that one colony, the Wilson colony in southern Alberta, had a net profit of over $1 million. I am searching for the facts here to make sure that my memory does not play tricks on me. It reads:
The balance sheet as December 31, 1970 shows assets in the amount of $1,235,855, liabilities in the amount of $1,060.
I wish that my little farm had so few liabilities. They had a net profit for that year of $107,697. So let us not be led astray by some bleeding hearts who think they know about religion and who feel akin to the Hutterites because they may have stemmed from Mennonite stock. We all stem from one stock or another but we are not all in competition with our brethren in the field of agriculture as these people are, and without a doubt they are in the business. When I can pick up a judgment and quote from it a statement that one colony alone had a net profit in 1970 of $107,000, we know we are not really dealing with a small entity. This is the profit of just one out of 83 colonies in the province of Alberta, and there are some 78 other colonies in the other two prairie provinces.
In other speeches I have dealt with whether or not one could call the Hutterites good citizens and whether or not they accept Canadian citizenship. I will not go into that subject because each man can form his own opinion as to what makes a good Canadian citizen and what does not. In my opinion, they do not fulfill the requirements of a good citizen. My three sons all grew up and went through 4-H. They recited the 4-H pledge pretty regularly, and they were told by their instructors that that is what constitutes a good citizen. The very attempt not to pay Canada Pension Plan contributions suggests to me that they are not

good citizens. But I do believe that parliament was very negligent in not calling them as witnesses before the committee and asking them what in their minds constitutes good citizenship so that they could defend themselves.
I began my remarks by making the point which I just made. It is a habit of mine in making speeches to conclude by returning to the point I made at the beginning, and that is what I am doing on this occasion. I hope that throughout this speech I made members aware of what the problem is. This bill will not pass today, I can assure the House of that, but it may be passed next week if this session carries on that long. I hope that future members of parliament will not have to take action similar to the one I had to take in 1961 to correct a wrong which had been perpetrated on the agricultural industry until 1961 which allowed a segment of the agricultural industry to grow, prosper, and yet pay no income tax. We should make sure that restitution is made and that everyone is taxed for the purpose of the Canada Pension Plan.
I see Mr. Speaker is about to rise to point out that my time has expired. I have spoken on this subject at length, and I do not suppose that much more would convince those members who have failed to even attempt to compromise in this difficult situation. I do not suppose that many more words would change the minds of members of this House, but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I will continue to attempt to change the minds of hon. members this afternoon at greater length than I have this morning.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIONS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to spend a little time supporting the amendment, which I had the honour to second, proposed by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). First of all, it is with some trepidation that I will attempt to correct the record as laid down by the hon. member for Crowfoot, but I think that in all fairness the House should be aware of the full import of the bill before us when we consider the amendment.
The hon. member for Crowfoot mentioned the requirements of the law with regard to social insurance numbers. When I spoke on the predecessor to this bill in July last, when the government made its first attempt to exempt these religious sects, I pointed out that I was a contributor to the Canada Pension Plan but probably would not be able to receive any benefits from it because I have always been opposed to the idea of a social insurance number. Personally, I have not applied for or received one, notwithstanding the strictures of the law as it reads at present.
At that time it was my understanding that the Department of National Revenue was responsible for enforcing this provision. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) was in the House on that occasion, and I challenged him to prosecute me, if he wished, for failing to obey the law. As a matter of conscience, Mr. Speaker, I do not see why I should be required to have a social insurance number.
As I understand the provisions of the bill now before us they remove the requirement that one must have a social
May 3, 1974

insurance number in order to receive benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. That at least should remove some of the objections raised by the Hutterian brethren to this plan. I gather their main objection was that they, too, felt they should not have social insurance numbers, yet were obliged to support this plan from which they would get no benefit, and they felt they should be exempt from the program. As I say, if the government now recognizes that Deople should no longer be compelled to have social insurance numbers, that goes a long way toward meeting the objections of the Hutterian brethren.
I think that confirms the mistake that this parliament has made so far in dealing with this bill because, as pointed out by the hon. member for Crowfoot, the Hutterian brethren and the other sects that wish to be exempted should be called before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to make their positions abundantly clear, and to give the facts on which they base their requests for exemption. This information should be made available to members of the House. I suppose those sects have already made it available to the minister, because somewhere along the line this idea germinated in the minister's mind. I would not suggest that it suddenly appeared like the electric light bulb that is switched on in comic strips to indicate the birth of an idea. There must have been some pressure applied from some place. Generally, the government does not initiate action without some reason, but so far I have been given no information to indicate why these religious sects should be exempted.
The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), when he spoke on this subject on second reading of the bill, displayed an abysmal ignorance of the situation, something which I found quite surprising because he is supposed to be the official critic on this side of the House.
He talked about the Mennonites who are so active in religious work in India, and he said that this was a wonderful thing they did. Mr. Speaker, it is a wonderful thing. I happen to have the honour to represent a great number of people who adhere to the Mennonite religion, and as I have said previously I cannot think of a finer identifiable group in my constituency. These people pay their way. They do not cause trouble. They are great adherents to the principles of voluntaryism. I cannot think of a better community in my constituency than the community surrounding Acme and Linden, but I do not think the people who go to the Mennonite church at Linden are the ones who want to be exempted from the Canada Pension Plan. Neither do I believe that the people who are doing such good work in the mission field in India and other places are the ones who want to be exempted from the Canada Pension Plan.
The hon. member for Crowfoot has referred to those who want to be exempt as the Amish people from western Ontario. He has made certain remarks about that group. I, for one, am unfamiliar with them, but if he is correct in saying they neither contribute to nor partake in our system of government, there could be some reason for exempting them from this program. But I think it would be a terrible mistake for us to proceed on an incorrect understanding of the facts.
I think that our spokesman on this side of the House, the hon. member for Hillsborough, has done a very poor job in
Canada Pension Plan
researching the position of this party with regard to this bill, and I must take exception to him. As I have said, these people should have been called and made to justify their position, because I think it is quite clear to anybody who has studied the Canada Pension Plan that it is not an actuarially sound program. And if it is not actuarially sound there will have to be extensive subsidies pumped into it in order to keep it afloat. Where are those subsidies to come from? They have to come from the general taxpayer, from the consolidated revenue fund. May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At one o'clock the House took recess.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIONS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose for lunch at one o'clock, I was dealing with the motion before the House, and particularly the actuarial soundness of the Canada Pension Plan. It is my opinion that the plan is not actuarially sound and further, the more the base is narrowed, the less sound the plan becomes.
I readily admit that the number of people we are considering in this part of the bill is not large. The Old Order of Mennonite Brethren is not a large group. The Hutterian Brethren is another matter. During his remarks, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) gave some information about the number of people involved in that sect. While it may not be large now, it is a rapidly growing group, particularly when one considers that that group doubles in size every 17 years, according to the information given by the hon. member by Crowfoot. I presume that if the facts the hon. member has given are wrong somebody more learned than he, and with some basis for saying so, will stand up in this House and put the record straight. Until that happens, I guess we will have to accept the information given by that hon. member.
With regard to the actuarial soundness of the plan, I wish to quote from an article that appeared in the October 20, 1973 edition of the Financial Post and headlined "Happy Birthday, David, and congrats". The article was written by James L. Clare, a Toronto actuary and corporate tax consultant. I quote:
Federal NDP leader David Lewis could ripoff the Canada Pension for at least $14,157.
David Lewis turns 65 on June 23, 1974, and will then be eligible for a $99-a-month CPP pension. Statistical odds suggests he can then expect to live 14 years, or 168 months.
His CPP contributions for the eight and a half years since the plan began, Jan. 1, 1966, will then total $1,435. These contributions will pay for almost 15 of those $99 monthly benefits. Interest will pay for about another 10 months of benefits. For the other 143 remaining months he can expect to live, his benefits will be paid from the CPP funds contributed by us folks still working, as a subsidy or gift to David

May 3, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
Lewis, i.e., as a ripoff. The 143 months of $99 ripoffs come to a total expected ripoff of $14,157.
Rather juicy, what?
Consider a Canadian of the same age who has been paid much less, and covered by the CPP for the same 814 years, but who year by year has earned one half of the CPP maximum covered earnings. His total contributions of $626 will pay for almost 13 of his $49.50 monthly benefits. Interest will pay for about another nine months of benefits. The benefits for the remaining 146 months he can expect to live will give him a total expected CPP subsidy of just $7,227.
David Lewis will be subsidized much more than the poor man- $6,930 more.
In a word, the CPP is "upside-down welfare."
Mr. Trudeau, why are the proposed CPP amendments of your government aiming at ballooning the subsidized ripoffs to the rich still further, with crumbs from the CPP to the poor and to the elderly? Why are you in such a hurry to line the pockets of Mr. Lewis still more?
Mr. Davis,-
I presume he is referring to the premier of Ontario.
-the CPP cannot legally be amended without the consent of your Ontario government-so why are you even more enthusiastic than Ottawa in urging even bigger subsidies and windfalls to the rich? What has Mr. Lewis done for you lately?
The CPP subsidies are silly, and if amended will be even sillier. Would it not make sense instead to amend the CPP so that the monthly dollar subsidies are (a) at least as much for the poor as for the rich, and (b) at least as much for older pensioners as for younger pensioners?
Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Davis, do your men really know what they are advocating? Maybe someone, somewhere, should look at all the facts first, before the CPP is changed in any way?
I think it is clear there is a serious problem with this plan. However, I think there is an even more serious problem facing the country today. The egg producers of Canada are suffering as a result of the importation and dumping of eggs in this country. The government says it needs amendments to the Export and Import Permits Act and has proposed Bill C-4. They made some reference to being willing to proceed with this piece of legislation today. I do not know whether the amendments are actually necessary before the government can act, but the government says they are. That legislation is of much higher priority than the legislation we are now discussing. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Horner):
That this debate be now adjourned.

speechtext:
Well, we have certainly proved that point. The government is not prepared to debate Bill C-4. The government had the opportunity and they failed to take it.
There are other things far more important than the measure we are considering. Members on this side made it clear months ago that this legislation would not, in all likelihood, be passed unless clause seven concerning special exemptions for religious sects was removed. But the government carried on with it. Today it is wasting time again, though it could be getting on with other legislation of greater importance. I think the minister responsible for arranging the business to come before the House knows this bill is put forward as a filler while the House is waiting for the budget to be brought down. They are afraid to bring anything else forward.
A motion has been put forward to delete that part of the bill which would give special consideration to a religious sect. I fully support the idea that special consideration should be given to religious sects in certain circumstances. After all, I grew up with a community of people who had emigrated here from Russia, the Doukhobors. They were granted special consideration based on their religion. They have contributed a tremendous amount to this country, and I think they are fairly happy about their freedom to practice their religion. But the crux of the matter is this: we are dealing with a bill concerning contributions to the Canada Pension Plan. In no way does this interfere with anyone practising or maintaining a religious belief. I can mention other things which are contrary to Hutterite practices-I mention the Hutterites because they are primarily the people involved in this case. It is contrary to their religious beliefs to watch television or listen to radio. Yet they pay taxes which go, in part, toward the maintenance of the CBC. They do not watch CBC programs because, in their minds, it is very sinful to do so. They may have a point there, Mr. Speaker. But ought we to rebate to them that particular portion of the tax?
To say they must contribute to the Canada Pension Plan in no way infringes upon religious freedom. And we are not talking about a poor, struggling people trying to maintain churches or build church halls. The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) mentioned 73 communities numbering, possibly, six or seven thousand people, and reporting a net profit of some $6 million. These are the people who are asking that they should be exempted from the Canada Pension Plan provisions.
This is what the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) stated in his speech, as reported at page 1482 of Hansard for April 16:
I may say the government still firmly believes in the universal application of programs such as the Canada Pension Plan. It firmly believes in the universality of a pension plan. But it considers an exemption should be made because it is in keeping with a strong tradition of freedom and tolerance which exists in this country.
Mr. Speaker, I am a great one for tolerance and personal freedom, like many other farmers. But I, like many other farmers, was given no choice about whether or not I would
May 3, 1974

keep books for my operation. I was forced to do so by law. We were not asked whether we wished to deduct income tax with respect to the people who work for us. This duty was forced upon us and we had no choice. The government talks about treating these people with tolerance because there is a tradition of freedom. No one else has individual freedom. Certainly I think we should show them tolerance as far as their religion is concerned, but what we propose would in no way prevent them from practising their religion. Besides, it is basic to what democracy means. Democracy means going along with what 51 per cent of the people want. People who do not drive cars are still called upon to pay for the highways. I would point out, also, that these people are not bound to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan. They can choose to earn less than $600 a year. If they decide to earn more, they should fall into the same category as everyone else.
I could list a variety of examples. Suppose I had a choice of being exempt from education tax. If I could get back what I pay in education taxes I would be only too willing to educate my children myself. But I do not have that freedom. I live in a democracy, and democracy demands that 100 per cent of the people should do what 51 per cent of the people want to do. The Hutterites live in Canada and they are good citizens. But why exempt them while trying to carry on the principle of universality in all the other cases? It is a bad precedent, it is not necessary, and it is amazing to me that so few members can get up enough energy or enough courage to speak against it.
The Hutterites have been given special consideration with regard to education. They have been given the right to educate their children in their own way, on their colonies. I do not say it would be impossible for others to do something like this, but I believe it would be very difficult if I were living on a farm and said to the local school board: Please send me out a teacher; I have 21 children here, my own and those of a few people around here; we shall provide the building, you should provide the teacher. I think I would have a fair amount of trouble getting that privilege.
I have no quarrel with the Hutterite people. That is not what is at stake here. They raise a tremendous amount of produce and they use the land to the best of their ability. On the other hand, they contribute very little to our society. They stand in line outside the doctor's office, when necessary and they are right ready to buy the latest machines if they are likely to help them earn a faster dollar, but none of their children go to universities; none of their descendants become doctors. None of them try to solve the mystery of what causes cancer, or anything else. None of their children get past grade eight. Thus, they do not contribute to the country in the way many other people do and for this reason alone I find it difficult to understand why they should be granted special exemption from a scheme which is supposed to be universal.
On the same page of Hansard, page 1482, the minister is recorded as saying that religious sects formed after 1966 will not be exempt should they make a similar application. So, this bill practically singles out the Hutterites and a few others in the Mennonite and Amish sects, but primarily there is a strict exemption of a very small group of very, very wealthy people. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, having
Canada Pension Plan
one million acres in the province of Alberta. What would that land be worth in a few years? Perhaps $500 an acre, with land today selling anywhere from $150 to $250 an acre. I will leave hon. members to figure it out.
These are the people asking for, and the people the government is anxious to grant to, special consideration because they are a religious sect. It is not that their paying into the Canada Pension Plan would in any way prevent them from carrying on their religion. As I have said, it puzzles me greatly. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) has legislation ready to increase the cash advances on grain. I am ready to speak on this legislation. We have the import-export bill, too. Then he introduced a bill which was given first reading this morning to put into legislative form the September 12 last announcement with regard to government subsidies for grain consumed in Canada, to ensure that the farmers obtain $5 maximum for wheat consumed in Canada. So I fail to understand why the minister is prepared to sit all afternoon while we debate this particular legislation, and while it fails to pass the House.

ter. I said that since I was the representative here of my constituents I would sit among them so I could better understand their feelings toward his remarks, whether they agreed with him or not. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my motion is to allow married women to contribute to and receive benefits from the Canada Pension Plan. When I moved this amendment to the amending bill last year, I recognized then that it probably was not in order, but I moved it to bring attention to the problem. I think I have to say that some recognition has been given to this problem since the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has produced a discussion paper on the subject of housewives contributing to the Canada Pension Plan. The bill in relation to which the amendment was put before was pretty narrow, and I can understand why it was not found in order. I did not quibble with that ruling as I thought it was a proper one at that time.
However, Bill C-19 with which we are dealing is a much broader piece of legislation, and we find in the recommendations the following words:
-to provide in the manner prescribed for equality of status for males and females under the Act-
For that reason I feel my amendment is much closer to being in order this time than last time. Of course, it can probably be argued from the other side that 100 per cent or 300 per cent of nothing is still nothing. I recognize that the words "in the manner prescribed" are rather limiting, but I have always understood in respect of these recommendations that they should not set out the particulars of the bill before us. I would urge that because it is recommended there be equity of status as between males and females under this bill consideration should be given to my amendment. There is a large number of housewives in this
May 3, 1974

country who are female citizens and should have the right to expect coverage under the national pension plan.
I am attempting to bring this idea before the House by referring to that part of the recommendation which says that one of the purposes of this bill is to provide equality of status. In no way are we going to encourage that equality of status between males and females if we do not include housewives. Unless we include housewives, we will not meet the requirements of that recommendation and that recommendation will, therefore, be meaningless.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIONS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you rule on the amendment I should like to speak on this point of order. You are quite correct in that the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) did move the amendment in respect of Bill C-90. Mr. Speaker at that time felt that it did not fall within the ambit of the bill then before us. I draw to your attention that in this particular case we have a bill with a great deal more depth and one which particularly deals with the spouses, their contributions and the benefits these spouses may collect. One can look at Clauses 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30 and see that we are in fact dealing with contributions that a spouse may or may not make, and the benefits that one of the survivors of a marriage may collect.
I would also bring to your attention, before you make your ruling, that during the committee study of this particular bill more time and paper was used on the questioning of this aspect of what the amendment suggests than on anything else.
It is interesting to note also that at the time of the committee study the minister did not say he was opposed to this aspect, but said he felt the government needed more time to study it. He did not say he could not fit it into this bill. Many of the members of that committee wanted it fitted in and the minister said that he had discussed it with the provinces and wanted more time to study this aspect. In view of the desirability of getting this bill through before the election everybody seems to be talking about around here, I would urge that you not rule the amendment out of order.
During committee proceedings there was wide acceptance of the principle enunciated in the amendment. We could incorporate it in the bill and the beneficiaries of the act, particularly the housewives across Canada, would be better off. Before making your ruling on the grounds the last amendment was found out of order, I would urge that this bill is completely different and much broader in scope. I think this amendment does fall within the ambit of this bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIONS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Motion No. 3.
That Bill C-19, An Act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, be amended in Sub-clause 15(2) by deleting the words 'prescribed rate' at line 25 and substituting '7%'.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this motion one tends to become involved in the whole question of interest rates. In the old bill the rate was 6 per cent. The change that this bill is attempting to bring in is to a prescribed rate. Someone across the way said that is very commendable. I have always been interested in the Liberals and their interest rates, because I well remember the debate of 1966 when the Liberal government took office and placed a freeze on the interest rate of the banks. The government at that time then decided to have a floating rate. One could look up the debate, and some of the new Liberal members should do so.

Canada Pension Plan
At that time it was decided to have a floating rate which would be 114 per cent above the short-term bond rate. Now, we are dealing with a prescribed rate. The prescribed rate is bound to be the floating rate. In 1966, the bank rate was 6 per cent but the government decided to float the rate at 114 per cent above the rate on short-term bonds. I well remember the debate. The present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) was Minister of Finance at that time. He said that the interest rate might well go below 6 per cent. That was the wishful thinking of the Liberal government at that time. The short-term bond rate in that particular year went as high as 7.72 per cent and then fell to 4.3 per cent. So, the government said that 1% per cent above 4.3 per cent would place the prescribed rate at 6.05 per cent. It is interesting to note that the bill at that time was to apply for an interim period with a rate fixed at 7V4 per cent. Then, it was decided that the Bank Act should be amended to allow the bank to bring in any rate it saw fit.
Then, it was decided that for the first year of the freeing of the bank rate a prescribed rate of 714 per cent would be arranged. The government went on to explain how the rate would fluctuate after that on a formula of 1M per cent above the short-term bond rate. However, the short-term bond rate and the 114 per cent were below the 714 per cent rate so the government was in an embarrassing position at the time. Several members from the Conservative Party and some from the socialist party to my left spoke against the freeing of the interest rate for the banks. When one looks at corporate profits one finds that in the past seven or eight years it is the banks which have had the greatest profits. The major shareholders of the banks have reaped the benefit of these higher profits earned by high interest rates.
The amendment I am presenting today is the same amendment I filed in this House I believe in the debate in the fall of 1966 when the 6 per cent interest rate freeze was removed from the Bank Act. I said that the rate should be frozen at 7 per cent. This is what my amendment in this case says. If a person should be late in respect of his payments he should be charged a rate of 7 per cent and not a prescribed rate. I have a dreadful fear concerning what a prescribed rate means in the mind of the present Liberal government. The Liberal government of 1966 said that a prescribed rate was 114 per cent above the rate on shortterm bonds. Whenever I see a bill come before this House which gives the Liberal Party the right to decide the interest rate I become concerned. The rate in the old act clearly is 6 per cent per annum. In this case it is a prescribed rate. Recently we have seen the banks of Canada increase their interest rate by 1 Vi per cent approximately. Everyone in Canada, except perhaps a person with a great deal of security, is paying between 10 Vi and 11 Vi per cent for money. There are members of this House who believe that under the present government the prescribed rate could go to the sky.
I believe everyone should examine this question. The Bank of Canada recently announced that it would increase its rate on loans to the chartered banks to 814 per cent. Perhaps no one has looked up the amount of money the chartered banks have borrowed from the central bank. In 1973, they did not borrow a red nickel or any other kind of nickel, but because the central bank raised its rate to 8 Vi

per cent the chartered banks took it upon themselves to raise their rate by 12 per cent. Although I do not have the exact figures, I would estimate that there is a total debt of approximately $40 million across Canada, and if one calculates a lVi per cent increase on that one can see that interest rates are a very important subject. All of a sudden in order to cure inflation, so we were told, a higher interest rate was imposed.
I do not know what effect this will have on payments made under the Canada Pension Plan. I think most mistakes are made honestly and without deliberate intent. I think most late filings are made honestly without deliberate intent. Why do we have to give power to the government to establish a prescribed rate? This government believes in high interest rates. If they want to curtail inflation, there are plenty of ways of doing so without increasing interest rates. When I speak of interest rates I cannot help going back to the debate when we started this cycle of high interest rates in the fall of 1966.
What was Canada's problem in 1966? At that time we were mighty concerned about the rate of inflation. Inflation was running wild. The Bank of Canada wanted to charge a higher interest rate and so did the chartered banks. That was their cure for inflation. It was argued by others that higher interest rates do nothing but increase inflation. It is not my fault, not this bill's fault, and not necessarily the Liberal government's fault that high interest rates increase inflation. The reason for inflation is the credit economy in which we are living. How have we evolved this type of economy? Goods and money became plentiful, and we borrowed. Our credit became good and people lent us more and more money. Interest rates are part of the cost.
I say that putting a prescribed rate into this legislation will only increase the cost of the entrepreneur doing business in Canada today. In 1966 the argument was used that interest rates would curb inflation, and there is no question in my mind that at that time they contributed to inflation because the entrepreneur makes them part of his cost and wherever possible passes on that cost to the buying public. The small portion of the debt in Canada will also be passed on to the consumer in the end product. In fact, 3.6 per cent of the cost of the labour force in a given business is deducted or charged against the product that the business produces. The interest rate on that money is charged to the product. There is no question in my mind that we cannot suddenly stop the credit economy that we have evolved. One member of the Liberal Party was concerned about our credit economy and tried to start a cashex system-a novel idea, but for one reason or another it did not catch on with the public.
We have been led down the garden path, or hornswog-gled, to use a good western expression, into believing that a credit economy is a good thing. I find myself in that position. I have many debts. Because the interest rate went up, I, along with everybody else, will have to pay. The argument for the high interest rate in the fall of 1966 when the Bank Act was before parliament was that it would curtail inflation. The evidence is before this government that it did not curtail inflation one bit; in fact, it contributed to it.

I do not want to make a speech today on the increase in the interest rate and what steps could be taken to cure inflation. That is not the purpose of our debate this afternoon. But surely we should consider what my amendment would do. It provides clearly that in a small way it will curtail the rate of inflation. It is the old story. If you watch the little things, the big things will take care of themselves. That is an old and wise philosophy expressed to me by many old homesteaders on the prairies. There is no question that if we look after the pennies the dollars will accrue. How many times have you heard that expression? If we look after low interest rates we will be proving this point without a doubt. Banks will have to lend money to the entrepreneurs.
It does not concern me if the government sets out its principles in pieces of legislation and states that it believes in a 7 per cent rate of interest. I would appreciate it if parliament accepted this amendment and stated that we believe it would be one small step in the direction of reducing interest rates and inflation. If the government wants to curtail inflation, if they want to bring the banks into line, why do they not change section 72 of the Bank Act which allows banks to charge an interest rate as low as 12 per cent on what might be'called negotiable reserves? If they want to tighten up the economy, let them increase that rate to 15 per cent or 16 per cent. I will listen with interest to the budget to see whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) suggests that. If he does, he will be taking a concrete step toward curtailing inflation without increasing the burden on the taxpayers as this bill will do and as the Bank of Canada did some months ago.
Why do interest rates mean so much with reference to the Canada Pension Plan? I wonder how many Canadians have ever asked themselves who uses all the money that has been amassed under the Canada Pension Plan. Every province in Canada except Quebec has the opportunity to borrow money from the Canada Pension Plan, that portion of it which is over and above the amount needed to pay the premiums in the province. Every province has the right to borrow that money at the rate of about 5 per cent. It is interesting to note the heavy borrowings over the years by the provinces. I should point out that the province of Quebec pays at the same rate but collects its own contributions and does not have to borrow this money from the federal government at 5 per cent.
It is interesting to point out that when the question of interest rates came up in the committee, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) readily admitted that Quebec has a different rate of interest on their bonds. They collect a 10 per cent return on the money they lend under the Canada Pension Plan. All that my amendment does is to signify that the interest rate which the government should establish on all borrowings under the Canada Pension Plan should be 7 per cent. This is not impossible to achieve. It is an acknowledgement that 6 per cent interest rate may be too low and might have to be changed. But I am very afraid of legislation which will pass this House providing that there shall be only a prescribed rate, because in all the time I have been in Ottawa I have not been convinced that the Liberal Party understands the meaning of interest rates. There is no question about it; they believe in high interest rates. They have allowed the governor of the Bank of Canada to increase
Canada Pension Plan
interest rates. For the first time in Canadian history, bank rates are 10 per cent to 11 Vi per cent, depending on the borrower's credibility, the security he can offer and the amount of the loan. Let me assure you that most people pay 11 Vi per cent.
The Canadian banks, among the best banking businesses in the world, are making all kinds of money. The government has a moral obligation to tell the banks that it does not approve of this. Months ago the government should have called in the governor of the Bank of Canada and told him it would not approve the 814 per cent interest rate that he proposed at that time. The government could begin to move on interest rates this afternoon by accepting this small amendment which proposes quite clearly that the interest rate shall be 7 per cent.
I well remember when the Bank Act was amended to remove the freeze on interest rates which then stood at 6 per cent. The whole argument in favour of a floating interest rate was that the rate would come down. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, who was minister of finance at the time, said the rate would be pegged at 7 Vi per cent for a year but after the year we could conceivably see interest rates going below 6 per cent. What kind of folly was that? Does that kind of folly still exist in the government's mind?
The government has not learned anything, because it is still trying to cure inflation by increasing interest rates, rather than increasing the percentage of funds which banks are obliged to keep in reserve. The Canada Pension Plan has become one of the greatest sources of funds for the provinces. Most provinces used to go to New York for their financing. Now, with the exception of Quebec, they come to Ottawa. The province of Ontario has borrowed huge amounts of money from the Canada Pension Plan fund. It has borrowed as much as $590 million in one year at an interest rate of 5 per cent. Certainly it is getting a good deal in this way, using the Canadian taxpayers' money. I should not say it is using the Canadian taxpayers' money, but the Ontario taxpayers' money, because the contributions of provinces are accumulated in separate funds from which the provinces can borrow at 5 per cent.
If the government allowed a prescribed rate, this could provide greater contributions to the pension fund. In fact, we might be able to increase the amount of pension payable without increasing the premium. But we have decided that the rate should be pegged at 5 per cent. Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is anything wrong with pegging it at 7 per cent. That is slightly more than the provinces have to pay for money now, but surely we do not have to enforce a higher penalty than 2 per cent in this respect. The amount of money saved by the Ontario government because of the prescribed 5 per cent rate on borrowings over $500 million a year would be astronomical. I am using Ontario as an example because it has the biggest population and borrows the most money from the fund. On average it has borrowed more than $590 million each year for the past few years. I admit that back in 1966 it did not borrow so much. I am looking for the exact figures but I cannot lay my hands on them. In any case, by now the point should be clearly understood by hon. members that it is quite proper to provide in a piece of legislation that there be a

May 3, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
fixed interest rate. Of course, as we read the bill now it suggests a 6 per cent rate. I am suggesting a 7 per cent rate.
I well remember during debates in 1966 that we were told we had to raise interest rates otherwise money would not come into Canada. We were told that if we maintained a low interest rate, foreign money would not come into Canada, that American money would stay in the United States and Europe would attract investment because interest rates there were increasing. Since that time the complaint has been that we have too much foreign investment in Canada and should do something about it. If the government had accepted the advice offered by some of us in 1966 and frozen interest rates at 7 per cent, we might have encouraged a little foreign money to come to Canada but not as much as is now flooding in, with interest rates going to 1114 per cent. You cannot blame the free enterprise society in which we live if money pours into a country where interest rates go to 11 Vi per cent. I repeat that we would not have the large foreign investment that Canada now knows if our advice had been accepted in 1966. In this debate I am offering the same advice. I maintain that the rate should be frozen at 7 per cent. Let this bill be a signal to our society that we are going to freeze interest rates at 7 per cent, that we are going to take steps to bring down interest rates.
I well remember that in election speeches in 1957 and 1958 the Liberal Party was charged with being a high interest rate party. I was just a young fellow at that time and was not certain whether the accusation was true. But having spent a number of years in Ottawa I am convinced beyond the shadow of a doubt that it is a high interest rate party. One of the beautiful things about democracy is that governments must obey the wishes of parliament. This is particularly true of a minority government. We see compromises. We see agreements being reached. Back on the farm we would even say that deals were being made. Politicians are not supposed to use that expression, but with this minority government we see deals being made. Why can't the government come down off its high interest rates? I was going to say "high horse", but we are debating interest rates so I must stick to that subject. Why can't this government come down from their high horse? There I go again with a slip of the tongue. My hon. friend says it is the wrong horse too, and there is no doubt about that, Mr. Speaker. If we go to the people next week, I hope they bear in mind that the Liberal Party has been responsible for high interest rates ever since it removed the freeze in 1966. It is still the party of high interest rates. If they reject this small amendment wnich I propose, it will signify again that they want high interest rates on even the smallest loans.
In this afternoon's debate I shall take time to drill this point home because I really believe there will be an election next week. I know the Liberal Party wants to continue to govern. This morning I listened to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) speak about Petro-Can and I realized that he wants to govern. He is throwing out a compromise, a deal with the NDP right now. He wants to continue to govern. Nothing would do the Liberals more good on the hustings next week or

next month than to wave a little piece of paper saying, "We are a party of lower interest rates. We are starting to bring down interest rates. We took this prescribed rate out of the act and froze it at 7 per cent. That is where interest rates should be frozen today. And when we go back we are going to freeze the rate of the banks at 7 per cent." They are on their high horse and believe in high interest rates. They believe that somehow they have an exalted right to rule. They really do not care how badly they bleed the public, because they believe in the theory: Bleed them well and give them back the concentrated blood mix and they will somehow survive.
